summary: Defines an architecture framework and functional requirements for carrying signaling information, such as telephone call setup messages, over IP networks. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Phone systems send little control notes to set up calls. This describes a way to send those notes safely over the Internet.

questions: how to transport signaling over ip
how is ss7 carried over ip
what is a media gateway controller
subtitle: The architecture for carrying telephone-network signaling messages across IP networks.

tldr.problem: Telephone networks signal call setup with protocols such as SS7 and Q.931, and carrying those messages over IP needs agreed roles, interfaces and performance targets.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines functional entities (Signaling Gateway, Media Gateway Controller, Media Gateway), a three-part Signaling Transport stack, and functional and performance requirements drawn from existing SCN protocols.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational framework that sets scope and requirements for signaling transport rather than a protocol, and it recommends IPSEC or an equivalent for security.

today: RFC 2719 is an Informational memo from October 1999 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a framework and requirements document, not a protocol specification.

sections.title: Overview and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 2719 defines an architecture framework for transport of message-based signaling protocols over IP networks. The scope covers encapsulation methods, end-to-end protocol mechanisms and use of existing IP capabilities. The framework part describes how functional and physical entities relate, and the requirements part covers needs such as flow control and in-sequence delivery.

Signaling Transport (SIG) means a protocol stack that carries signaling from a Switched Circuit Network (SCN), such as the public telephone network, over IP. The transport is meant to be transparent, so the SCN protocols themselves, interworking such as converting channel associated signaling to message signaling, and the internal functions of the gateway units are out of scope.

It shall be used between a Signaling Gateway Unit and a Media Gateway Controller Unit, and may also be used between a Media Gateway Unit and a Controller Unit, between dispersed Controller Units, and between two Signaling Gateway Units.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone network and the Internet speak different languages. This memo is only about carrying the phone network's notes across the Internet unchanged, not about translating them.

sections.title: Functional Entities and Gateway Models
sections.content:
The model splits a gateway into three functions. A Signaling Gateway (SG) receives and sends SCN native signaling at the edge of the IP network and may relay, translate or terminate SS7. A Media Gateway Controller (MGC) handles registration and management of resources at the Media Gateway (MG), which terminates SCN media streams and packetizes them. Each function can sit in its own physical unit (SGU, MGCU, MGU) or be combined.

For SS7 interworking, the SG terminates the SS7 link and hands signaling to the MGC using Signaling Transport, while the MG terminates the trunk. In one case the SG function is co-located with the MG, and signaling is backhauled to the controller. The SG role can also be divided across several units, so one SS7 layer, for example MTP3, can be carried between SG1 and SG2, and another, for example ISUP, between SG2 and the MGC.

For ISDN, the Q.931 signaling channel travels with the data channels, so the SG function sits with the MG and Signaling Transport carries Q.931 to the MGC. For database access, TCAP over IP supports cross-access between SS7 and IP domains, for example from an SS7 network to a Service Control Point in IP.
sections.plainLanguage: Picture a post office with three jobs: one clerk reads the control notes, one boss decides what to do, and one worker moves the actual voice. The notes travel between the clerk and the boss over the Internet.

sections.title: The Signaling Transport Protocol Stack
sections.content:
Signaling Transport is assumed to have three components: an adaptation sub-layer with the primitives a particular SCN signaling application needs, a Common Signaling Transport Protocol providing a common set of reliable transport functions, and a standard, unmodified IP transport protocol underneath.

The memo shows this stack in several access cases: SS7 access for media gateway control (ISUP carried between SG and MGC), ISDN Q.931 access to the MGC, SS7 access to an IP signaling endpoint where either SCCP or a whole SS7 Application Part is carried, and SG to SG cases where the carried layer is MTP3 or ISUP. When an SS7 Application Part is carried, SIG must support both the TC-user and the SCCP-user interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: The stack is like a parcel: the phone note goes in a labeled envelope, a courier service makes sure it arrives in order, and ordinary Internet delivery carries it.

sections.title: Functional and Performance Requirements
sections.content:
Signaling Transport shall carry a variety of SCN protocols (SS7 MTP Level 3, ISUP, SCCP, TCAP, MAP, INAP, IS-41, and Q.931 and QSIG), identify which one is carried, and define a common base protocol with header formats, security extensions and procedures. Together with IP it must provide the functionality of the SCN lower layer, such as flow control, in-sequence delivery, error detection, retransmission, failure recovery and detection of unavailable peers. It must also multiplex several SCN sessions on one transport session, carry messages longer than SCN segmentation limits, support a range of security schemes, and avoid congestion.

In-sequence delivery is required within a single control stream, but not necessarily across different streams, so the protocol should avoid blocking one stream because of a sequence error in another.

The performance targets come from existing signaling specifications. MTP Level 3 peer procedures need a response within 500 to 1200 ms. For MTP Level 3 user part messages, no more than 1 in 10E+7 messages may be lost, no more than 1 in 10E+10 delivered out of sequence, and availability of a route set is 99.9998% or better. Payload length is 272 bytes for narrowband SS7 and 4091 bytes for broadband SS7. ISUP's continuity test needs a returned tone within 2 seconds, and Q.931 round-trip delay should not exceed 4 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone notes must arrive fast, in the right order, and almost never get lost. The memo writes down exactly how fast and how reliable, based on the rules phone networks already follow.

sections.title: Management and Security
sections.content:
Management of IP or SCN networks (OA&M), for example legacy telephony systems or SNMP managers, is outside the scope of SIGTRAN.

For security, signaling kept within an intranet uses security at the network owner's discretion, but signaling crossing the public Internet should be treated as insecure and security measures are required. The aspects listed are authentication, integrity, confidentiality (sometimes) and availability.

No new security mechanism needs to be defined in SIG, since existing ones are sufficient. IPSEC (RFC 2401) with its AH and ESP protocols works with either TCP or UDP underneath, can use IKE (RFC 2409) for key distribution, but may be troubled by NAT if SIG embeds IP addresses outside the IP header. SSL and TLS (RFC 2246) work only over TCP. IPSEC or an equivalent is recommended, especially over the public Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Call-setup notes must not be forged or read by strangers. Using the Internet's existing locks, like IPSEC, is enough, and the memo says to use them when notes cross the public Internet.
